ai.definition: Agentic Workflow Orchestrators are AI systems designed to autonomously plan, execute, and correct multi-step business processes. These systems leverage large language models (LLMs) combined with the ability to interface with legacy APIs through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), enabling them to operate without hard-coded scripts.
ai.howItWorks: These orchestrators use LLMs to understand and interpret complex business rules and requirements, then execute these processes by interacting with various enterprise systems via API calls. They can also monitor the execution of tasks and correct any deviations from expected outcomes in real-time.
ai.problemSolved: Manual intervention in multi-step business processes is inefficient and error-prone. Agentic Workflow Orchestrators automate these processes to improve efficiency, reduce costs, and minimize errors.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves developing the software architecture, training LLMs on relevant data, integrating with various enterprise systems, and ensuring robust API interactions.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes data collection, model training, system integration, testing, and deployment. It requires a combination of AI development skills, domain expertise in business processes, and IT infrastructure knowledge.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the initial investment in LLMs and RAG technology, ongoing maintenance costs for APIs and systems, and continuous data updates to ensure model accuracy.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is positive as enterprise adoption of AI-driven process automation continues to grow. However, challenges such as integration with legacy systems and ensuring data privacy may slow widespread acceptance.
ai.regulation: Regulations around data privacy (e.g., GDPR) and cybersecurity must be strictly adhered to. Compliance can increase costs but is essential for trust in these systems.
ai.risks: Risks include potential inaccuracies in process execution, security vulnerabilities due to API interactions, and the need for constant updates as business processes evolve.
ai.profitability: Profitability depends on successful implementation by enterprises willing to automate complex workflows. High initial costs may limit immediate profitability but can lead to significant long-term savings.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may include enhanced integration with newer technologies like edge computing and blockchain, further improving efficiency and security.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and data center operations.

glossary.def: Large language model, a type of AI model used for generating human-like text.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation, an approach where LLMs use retrieved information from a database to enhance their responses.

subsystems.name: Model layer
subsystems.role: the reasoning engine — one or more large language models, often with a router that sends easy steps to a small cheap model and hard steps to a large one.

subsystems.name: Planning and control loop
subsystems.role: decides what to do next, observes the result, and revises the plan until the goal is met or it gives up.

subsystems.name: Tool and action layer
subsystems.role: the agent's hands: typed interfaces to real systems.
parts: connectors to internal and third-party APIs

subsystems.name: Memory and retrieval
subsystems.role: gives the agent facts it was not trained on and a record of what it has already done.

subsystems.name: Orchestration and state
subsystems.role: keeps long, multi-step runs alive across failures, restarts and waits.
parts: durable execution engine with persisted state

subsystems.name: Guardrails and permissions
subsystems.role: limits what the agent is allowed to touch.

subsystems.name: Evaluation and observability
subsystems.role: makes the system measurable instead of a demo.
parts: end-to-end traces of every model call and tool call
labelled task sets and regression suites

buildSteps.title: Map the process and its decision points
buildSteps.detail: Write down the current workflow step by step, mark where judgement is required and where a rule suffices, and define what a correct finished outcome looks like.

buildSteps.title: Expose the tools
buildSteps.detail: Wrap each system the agent must touch in a narrow, well-described interface. Integration work is still done by hand — the agent chooses and sequences calls, it does not invent connectors.

buildSteps.title: Choose and benchmark models
buildSteps.detail: Run candidate models on a sample of real tasks, measuring accuracy, latency and cost per run, and pick a router policy rather than a single model.

buildSteps.title: Build retrieval
buildSteps.detail: Ingest the policies, tickets, contracts or records the agent must read; chunk them, embed them and index them so relevant passages can be fetched at run time.

buildSteps.title: Implement the control loop
buildSteps.detail: Code the plan-act-observe-replan cycle with an explicit step limit, so the agent cannot loop forever or spend without bound.

buildSteps.title: Add durable state
buildSteps.detail: Persist the run's state after each step so that a crash, a restart or a three-day wait for an approval does not lose the work or repeat a side effect.

buildSteps.title: Wire permissions and guardrails
buildSteps.detail: Give each run its own scoped identity, restrict it to a list of permitted actions, and insert approval gates before anything irreversible such as payments or deletions.

buildSteps.title: Evaluate, then shadow-run
buildSteps.detail: Score the agent against the labelled task set, then run it alongside humans in read-only mode and compare its proposed actions with what staff actually did.

buildSteps.title: Expand autonomy gradually
buildSteps.detail: Enable write actions one at a time, starting with low-consequence ones, and keep humans in the loop until measured success rates justify removing them.

prerequisites.tech: Language models with reliable tool calling
prerequisites.why: the agent needs structured output naming a function and its arguments, not free prose.
enterprise facts are private and change, so they must be fetched rather than memorised in weights.
business processes run for hours or weeks and must survive restarts without duplicating side effects.
agents that write and run code need isolation so a mistake cannot reach production systems.
open schemas for exposing tools are young, so much integration remains bespoke per vendor.
a run can be right for the wrong reasons, and no widely accepted benchmark captures long-horizon enterprise work.

pathway.milestone: single-domain agents that draft or recommend, with a human approving every write
pathway.unlocks: measurable time savings on document-heavy, rule-bounded work.

pathway.milestone: agents that complete whole tasks in a narrow domain and escalate only the exceptions
pathway.unlocks: headcount can be redirected from processing to review.

pathway.milestone: long-running agents with persistent memory and replayable state across systems and weeks
pathway.unlocks: processes too long for a single session, such as onboarding or procurement cycles.

pathway.milestone: agents from different organisations negotiating through shared tool protocols
pathway.unlocks: automated transactions between companies, contingent on identity, liability and audit standards.
